title: Delhi HC Sets Aside Award on Zee-Religare Loans, Rejects Maharashtra Stamp Act
seo_title: Delhi HC: Stamp Duty Follows Where Deed Is Completed
meta_description: Delhi HC sets aside a Zee-Religare loan arbitration award, holding stamp duty follows where the agreement was completed, not first signed.
case_name: Asian Satellite Broadcast Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. v. Religare Finvest Limited & Anr. (common judgment with seven connected petitions)
body: In March 2014, Religare Finvest Limited lent money to four companies in the Zee Group under four loan agreements, each dated 15 March 2014. The borrowers allegedly stopped repaying, and Religare invoked the arbitration clause. What should have been a straightforward recovery arbitration instead turned into more than a decade of litigation over a question that had nothing to do with whether the money was owed: which state's stamp law applied to the loan agreements, Maharashtra's or Delhi's, under the Indian Stamp Act.

The first arbitrator, in 2020, held that the Maharashtra Stamp Act governed and directed Religare to get the agreements adjudicated by the Collector of Stamps there. That ruling itself went up to the Delhi High Court and then to the Supreme Court, which dismissed the Zee Group's challenge in April 2022 and, through orders in May and September 2022, sent the stamp-law question back to the arbitral tribunal to decide afresh, this time with a successor arbitrator in charge. That tribunal framed the stamp-law question as a preliminary issue and, on 28 February 2026, passed an interim award once again holding that the Maharashtra Stamp Act applied and that a fixed duty of Rs. 100 applied to each agreement under Article 5(h)(B) of its Schedule I.

Religare challenged that interim award under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, filing four separate petitions. The Zee Group companies filed four petitions of their own defending the award. Justice Om Prakash Shukla heard all eight together and delivered a common judgment. Before getting to the merits, he dealt with a threshold objection: that a ruling on which stamp law applies is really a jurisdictional question under Section 16 of the Act, and that Sections 16(5) and (6) bar an immediate challenge to it. The judge rejected that framing, holding that which stamp law governs a contract is a pure question of law rather than a question about the tribunal's own jurisdiction, and that the preliminary issue had in any case been framed pursuant to the Supreme Court's own directions rather than in furtherance of a jurisdictional objection under Section 16.

On the substance, the arbitrator's award had treated the Maharashtra Stamp Act as applicable because the Zee Group borrowers, based in Mumbai, had signed the loan agreements first, before the documents were sent to Religare in Delhi for countersignature. The Delhi High Court rejected that reasoning. An agreement, the court held, is 'executed' at the place where it is completed by the last necessary signature, not at the place where the first party happened to put pen to paper. Since Religare's signature in Delhi was what made each agreement binding, the agreements were executed in Delhi, and it is the Indian Stamp Act as it applies in the National Capital Territory that governs them, not Maharashtra's statute.

Having found the Maharashtra Stamp Act inapplicable, the court set aside the interim arbitral award of 28 February 2026 in its entirety. It allowed Religare's four petitions and dismissed the four filed by the Zee Group companies, with no order as to costs. The stamp-law question, which has now been litigated through two rounds before the arbitral tribunal, an earlier round before the High Court, and an appeal to the Supreme Court, is left to be revisited by the tribunal in light of this finding before the underlying recovery dispute itself can move forward.

The principle the court applied has a reach well beyond this one loan dispute. Commercial agreements routinely get signed by parties sitting in different cities, sometimes different countries, and it is common for one side to sign first and courier the document on for countersignature. Treating the first signatory's location as decisive would let a party pick which state's, or in a cross-border contract which country's, stamp regime applies simply by choosing where to sign first, something a court is unlikely to accept once the point is put to it squarely. Lenders, borrowers and anyone drafting a multi-city facility agreement now have a clearer answer: stamp duty follows the place where the contract becomes binding on completion, not an accident of signing order.
why_it_matters: Loan and facility agreements signed by parties in different states are common, and which state's stamp duty applies can change the fee payable and even the document's admissibility in court. This ruling confirms that execution happens where the last signature completes the contract, not wherever the first party signed, which matters for lenders and borrowers structuring multi-city financing and for anyone drafting or stamping a cross-location commercial agreement.
card_summary: Delhi HC sets aside a decade-old stamp duty finding in the Religare-Zee loan arbitration, holding the loan agreements were executed in Delhi because that is where the last signature completed them.
card_tip: A multi-party agreement is stamped as executed where the last signature completes it, not wherever the first party signed.
